1.pericope_label: Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred

schools.summary: Ellicott opens with the source question nobody else asks — no eye-witness was present, so the account must be myth, revelation, or Christ's own report — and argues for the last, since a legend built on Genesis would have kept the serpent and the trees, and the differing order of the temptations tells against a supernatural revelation. He then reads the leading of the Spirit as an ecstasy 'in which the ordinary phenomena of consciousness and animal life were in great measure suspended'. Robertson keeps to a strong impulsion sending Jesus out to think through what his baptism committed him to; Barnes locates the fear in the learning and splendour of the city; Lightfoot alone supplies a calendar, mid-Tisri onward, so that Jesus 'conflicted with cold, as well as want and Satan'.

Calvin gives two reasons for the withdrawal — that Christ might come forth 'as a new man, or rather a heavenly man', and might undergo an apprenticeship before so arduous an office — with Moses on Sinai as the parallel. He denies the fast was an exercise of temperance at all, since there was no virtue in refusing food 'for which he had no more appetite than if he had not been clothed with flesh', and turns that into an attack on Lent as 'mere folly'. Gill finds it 'very surprising' that no hunger attended the whole forty days.

Clarke supplies the rabbinic answer to how any man could fast so long — in any city one lives by its customs, and Moses 'ascended to heaven, where they neither eat nor drink' — and links the combat to the promise that the seed should bruise the serpent's head, observing that 'the first act of the ministry of Jesus Christ was a combat with Satan'. Wesley states the pastoral rule in a line: after the clearest light, expect the sharpest temptation.

Henry calls the episode 'a famous duel, fought hand to hand, between Michael and the dragon', the heel bruised and the head broken, and draws from the word then the warning that high privilege is no security: 'the enriched soul must double its guard.'

Chrysostom gives five reasons why God does not hinder temptation — to prove the man stronger than he knew, to keep him modest, to convince the demon he is forsaken, to temper him 'better than any steel', and to display the treasures entrusted to him — resting on the premise that 'the devil would not have assailed thee, unless he had seen thee brought to greater honor'. Pseudo-Chrysostom makes the wilderness a second baptism, by fire instead of water.

debates.question: Where did the narrative of the Temptation come from?

positions.view: From Christ's own lips to a disciple. No eye-witness was present; myth is excluded because a legend would have reused the serpent and trees of Genesis and because the expected Messiah was a king rather than a sufferer; miraculous revelation is excluded because the evangelists are compilers and their orders differ.

debates.question: What state was Christ in when the Spirit led him?

positions.view: Something 'more or less of the nature of ecstasy', on the analogy of John in the Spirit, Ezekiel lifted up and Philip caught away, with ordinary consciousness largely suspended.
A strong impulsion by the Holy Spirit, driving him out to think through the significance of the step he had taken.
'Probably through a strong inward impulse' — nothing more is claimed.

debates.question: Did Christ feel hunger during the forty days?

positions.view: No — Gill calls it 'very surprising' that none attended the whole time, Robertson quotes Alford that 'the wants of the natural body were suspended', and Calvin uses the point to deny the fast was an act of abstinence at all.
The closing words mark 'a partial return to the common life of sensation', the cravings at last giving the tempter his opening.

outliers.view: Turns the forty days into a polemic against Lent: to appoint such a fast in imitation of Christ 'is mere folly', since neither Moses nor Christ kept one yearly but once in a lifetime, and the imitators 'stuff their belly so completely at dinner, that, when the hour of supper arrives, they have no difficulty in abstaining from food'.

themes: Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil.
And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred.

3.pericope_label: And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread

schools.summary: Ellicott refuses to visualise the tempter at all: nothing suggests 'a bodily presence visible to the eye of sense', and attempts to supply one — Milton's, or the rationalists' scribe or priest — 'diminish our sense of the reality and mystery of the Temptation'. He then makes the temptation layered, part Esau's question about the birthright, part an inference from Sonship to lordship over nature, part a public establishing of standing. Robertson reads the conditional as assuming its own truth, the devil quoting the baptismal voice back at Christ, and pictures him holding up a stone. Barnes insists neither Moses nor Christ meant spiritual food, the Hebrew word meaning thing; Jamieson calls Deuteronomy 8:3 the most apposite passage available and puts the conclusion in Christ's mouth: 'as man, therefore, I will await divine supply.'

Calvin loses patience with the tradition that made the three temptations gluttony, ambition and covetousness — 'ingenious trifles', since nothing is intemperate in a starving man wanting food — and holds instead that 'Satan made a direct attack on the faith of Christ'. He agrees with the grammarians that the spiritual-food reading tortures the text to a false meaning, and turns the use of Scripture into a weapon: Christ 'uses Scripture as his shield', and those who withhold it from the people 'deprive them of their arms'. Gill grants the spiritual sense is 'a certain truth' but not the sense here.

Clarke concludes from the missing article that the devil was probing rather than certain — 'whatever Satan might suspect, he did not fully know that the person he tempted was the true Messiah' — and states the temptation in a sentence: 'distrust the Divine providence and support, and make use of illicit means to supply thy necessities.' He pushes the answer further than the others, so that even fasting at God's command 'becomes a mean of supporting that life which it seems naturally calculated to impair'. Wesley has the tempter appear visibly, 'probably in a human shape'.
Pseudo-Chrysostom reads the timing pastorally: the devil despaired at the fast and took heart at the hunger, so a man tempted after fasting should 'say not, I have lost the fruit of my fast'.

debates.question: Was the tempter visible?

positions.view: Yes — after forty days of secret suggestion he 'puts on a visible form, and with an articulate, audible voice', Wesley guessing a human shape.
No — nothing in the narrative suggests bodily presence, and the account is not less true for lying 'altogether in the spiritual region of man's life'.

debates.question: Did the devil know whom he was tempting?

positions.view: No — the missing article means he was probing; 'perhaps one grand object of his temptation was to find this out'.
He assumes it: the conditional is of the kind that grants its own premise, quoting the voice heard at the baptism back at Christ.

debates.question: What sin was being urged?

positions.view: Distrust — Calvin against the ancients' scheme of gluttony, ambition and covetousness, holding that Satan attacked the faith of Christ so as to drive him to unlawful means.

Something layered: Esau's contempt for a birthright, an inference from Sonship to lordship over nature, and a public establishing of Messianic standing — rejected as 'an act of self-assertion and distrust'.

debates.question: Does the answer from Deuteronomy concern spiritual food?

positions.view: No, though all three concede the doctrine is true elsewhere: the meaning here is that God is not tied to bread, as manna proved. Calvin says some 'torture it to a false meaning'.

outliers.view: Alone extends the answer to make fasting itself a means of life: undertaken at God's command it 'becomes a mean of supporting that life which it seems naturally calculated to impair or destroy'.

themes: And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread.
But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.

5.pericope_label: Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple

schools.summary: Ellicott adjudicates the differing order of the last two temptations in Matthew's favour, since 'Get thee behind me, Satan' belongs at the close, and reads the taking as 'outside the conditions of local motion', borrowing Paul's formula about the body. Barnes denies any bodily conveyance at all, showing from parallels that the verb means only to conduct or accompany, and rules out the temple roof because Josephus says it was set with golden spikes. Robertson explains Luke's order as geographical. On the height they differ without noticing — Barnes over seven hundred feet, Ellicott four hundred cubits, Robertson about four hundred and fifty. Lightfoot admits the site 'is in vain to seek, because it cannot be found'.

Calvin refuses both questions the others press. Which contest came second 'need not give us much trouble or uneasiness', since the evangelists did not set out to preserve exact order; and whether Christ was carried bodily he declines to settle — 'in a matter that is doubtful, and where ignorance brings no risk, I choose rather to suspend my judgment' — while noting that the showing of all the kingdoms 'agrees better with the idea of a vision'. On the temptation itself he sees the mirror of the first: having failed to drive Christ to despair, Satan now urges 'a foolish and vain confidence'. Gill holds firmly that the transport was 'not in a visionary way, but really and truly'.
Clarke identifies the pinnacle as the king's gallery and quotes Josephus on its vast height, from which a man looking down 'would grow dizzy'.

Pseudo-Chrysostom supplies the devil's reasoning between the rounds: from the first answer he 'could learn nothing certain whether He were God or man', so revised his estimate downward to a holy man who had subdued the flesh, and changed his line of attack.

debates.question: Was Christ physically carried to the pinnacle?

positions.view: Yes, really and truly — Satan by divine permission and Christ's consent had power to move his body, as the Spirit caught away Philip.
No — 'there is no evidence that Satan had power to do any of these things'; the verb means only to conduct or accompany.
The taking lies 'outside the conditions of local motion', like Ezekiel's visions: whether in the body or out of it cannot be said.
Suspends judgment, though noting the third temptation suits a vision better.

debates.question: Whose order of the temptations is right?

positions.view: Matthew's, on balance, since the dismissal of Satan belongs at the close; Luke's informant may have been less accurate, or impressions differed if the temptations recurred.
Luke's order is geographical, not chronological.
The question 'need not give us much trouble or uneasiness'; the evangelists wrote an abridged narrative, not a dated one.

debates.question: What was the point of the suggestion?

positions.view: Not a public wonder to win power and popularity: the answer shows it 'tended, not to vain glory, but to distrust simulating reliance'.
Presumption as the mirror of despair — Satan now urging Christ 'to throw himself, without necessity, into manifest danger'.

outliers.view: Brings up, from the Talmud and bearing on nothing in the argument, the priests who climbed to the temple roof when fire was first set to it and threw the keys of its chambers heavenward — 'because we are not worthy to keep these keys, to thee they are delivered' — a shape like a hand taking them before they leapt into the fire.

themes: Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple,

6.pericope_label: And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down... Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God

schools.summary: Robertson lists the whole technique in a line — 'the devil quotes the Word of God, misinterprets it, omits a clause, and tries to trip the Son of God by the Word of God' — and supplies the dimensions others pass over: the nervous dread of the height, and a populace that would take a man 'sailing down as if from heaven' for the Messiah, the angels serving as 'a spiritual parachute'. Ellicott rejects that public reading, holding the suggestion tended to distrust rather than display, and notices which words were weaponised — the verses turned into a snare 'must have been precisely those that had before been most precious'. He also corrects the preposition, better on the hands than in them.

Calvin meets the objection the misuse invites: if Scripture can be so turned, should it be distrusted? 'Nor ought we to imitate the madness of those who throw away Scripture, as if it admitted of every kind of interpretation, because the devil misapplies it. For the same reason, we ought to abstain from food, to avoid the risk of being poisoned.' He locates the fraud precisely in the omitted condition, since the guardianship belongs to those who 'keep themselves within their bounds', and answers that promises cannot be claimed apart from commands: those who abandon the means God gives 'act as absurdly as if one were to cut off a man's arms and hands, and then order him to work'. Gill notices that Christ declines to argue the misquotation at all.

Clarke sees the shape of the attack first — the answer that defeated the last temptation has become the ground of this one — and identifies the surgery on the quotation, the clause 'to keep thee in all thy ways' being left out 'as quite unsuitable to his design'. He then reads the promise itself with unexpected tenderness, as a nurse's management of a child, lifting it over obstacles and setting it down to walk again. Wesley adds only that the bearing up means great care.

debates.question: What was the temptation aiming at?

positions.view: Partly a public sign: a man seen descending from the temple would satisfy what the populace expected of a Messiah.
Not display but 'distrust simulating reliance' — the answer given shows the suggestion tended that way, not to vain glory.

debates.question: Where exactly does the misquotation cheat?

positions.view: Not in claiming angels for Christ, which is true, but in the omitted condition: the guardianship is promised to those who walk in their ways, so God commands the walking and then promises the angels, whereas Satan produces the angels to license a leap.
In the dropped clause 'to keep thee in all thy ways' — 'as the path of duty is the way of safety, they are entitled to no good when they walk out of it'.

outliers.view: Alone reads the bearing up in the angels' hands as domestic tenderness rather than power — 'a metaphor taken from a nurse's management of her child: in teaching it to walk, she guides it along plain ground; but, when stones or other obstacles occur, she lifts up the child, and carries it over them, and then sets it down to walk again'.

themes: And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.
Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.

8.pericope_label: Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them

schools.summary: Barnes takes the sight literally and reaches for the Abbé Mariti's summit overlooking Gilead, Moab, Jericho, Jordan and the Dead Sea, concluding that 'we must not suppose that there was any miracle when they were shown', the world here meaning Judea, whose three governments had rulers called kings. Ellicott treats the verse as settling the whole nature of the Temptation, since no mountain commands such a survey and Luke's 'in a moment of time' is a flash concentrating 'the work of years'; he half recommends Milton's expansion while calling it 'too obviously the work of a scholar exulting in his scholarship'. Robertson refuses to make the readings exclusive — the panorama 'had to be partially mental and imaginative', but that does not prove there was no objective presence. Lightfoot answers the question differently again, and Jamieson notes only what Matthew omits.

Calvin holds the two together with the chapter's most careful distinction. The effect on Christ's eyes was real, owed not to weakness of nature but 'to a voluntary dispensation and permission'; yet 'while his senses were moved and powerfully affected by the glory of the kingdoms which was presented to them, no inward desire arose in his mind' — Christ 'had the same feelings with ourselves, but he had no irregular appetites'. The offer he treats as theft, the devil 'robbing God of the government of the world', a fraud still practised by men who profess that every good comes from God yet 'make Satan the distributor of all the riches in the world'. Gill has him carried bodily to an unknown mountain.

Clarke argues for the limited sense on physical grounds — no mountain could show one hemisphere, 'and the other must of necessity be in darkness' — and suspects Matthew wrote the Hebrew word meaning equally the earth and the land. Wesley settles it in five words: 'a kind of visionary representation.'
Pseudo-Chrysostom reads the three assaults as nets — appetite broken, ambition passed over, covetousness now spread — and supposes the devil had noticed this mountain while going about the earth.

debates.question: What did Christ actually see?

positions.view: A real panorama from a real summit, the world meaning Judea and the neighbouring country, so that no miracle need be supposed.

Rome and her empire — that empire is called all the world by sacred and profane writers, other cities counted for little beside it, and Rome was 'the seat of Satan'; what was offered was the power of Caesar, which 'antichrist afterward obtained'.
Nothing bodily: no mountain commands such a view, so all of it 'was in the region of which the spirit, and not the senses, takes cognisance'.
Partially mental and imaginative, but that 'does not prove that all phases of the temptations were subjective without any objective presence of the devil. Both could be true.'

outliers.view: Draws the finest Christological distinction in the chapter: the senses were genuinely moved by the glory presented to them, 'yet no inward desire arose in his mind', since Christ 'had the same feelings with ourselves, but he had no irregular appetites'.

themes: Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them;

9.pericope_label: And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me... Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him

schools.summary: All three concede a good deal to the claim. Barnes allows it 'with considerable justice', Ellicott says it 'rested on the apparent evidence of the world's history' and that 'in part, the claim is allowed by our Lord's language', Robertson that 'Jesus does not deny the grip of the devil on the world of men'. Ellicott marks the change of target — no longer the sense of Sonship but 'the love of power' — and reads the changed formula as evidence that evil had until now come disguised, 'making sins of distrust appear as acts of faith'. Robertson borrows McNeile's threefold analysis and denies that 'behind me' belongs in the text here. Barnes explains the sharper tone by the sharper attack.

Calvin refuses to speculate about the phrase addressed to Peter 'as if the same words had not been addressed to Satan', and takes the answer as settling a much later argument: Rome concedes latreia to God alone while keeping an inferior douleia for 'dead men, and on their bones and statues', a distinction Christ destroys by claiming for God the very word that means bodily homage, so that 'not only the inward worship, but also the outward manifestation of it, is due to God alone'. He adds that Christ was never in fact forsaken by the angels, the grace present with him being 'sometimes hidden, so far as respects the feeling of the flesh'. Gill notes that mildness had been shown until the behaviour became intolerable.

Clarke sums the whole conflict as four attacks — distrust, presumption, worldly ambition, idolatry — holding that 'there is probably not a temptation of Satan, but is reducible to one or other of these four articles', and draws the consolation that being tempted while one resists is not sin, Christ himself having been tempted to worship the devil. Wesley notices that Christ now uses the enemy's own name, 'which he had not done before', and distinguishes this dismissal from the sending of Peter to his proper place.
Cyril presses the verb over the angels: Scripture 'saith not, they succoured Him, but they ministered unto Him, that is, like servants' — proof that the Son is Lord of angels.

debates.question: Was the devil's claim to the kingdoms valid?

positions.view: Partly — the kingdoms were wicked, the world's history bears the claim out, and Christ denies not the grip but only the condition attached.
It was theft: in claiming to bestow them the devil was 'robbing God of the government of the world, and claiming it for himself'.

debates.question: Is the reply 'get thee hence' or 'get thee behind me'?

positions.view: The longer reading is well attested — Clarke says it is added 'by a multitude of the best MSS., Versions, and Fathers'.
Those words 'belong to Matthew 16:23, not here'.
The difference is one of meaning: behind me would send Satan to his proper place, as it later sent Peter; this is simple dismissal.
Calvin refuses to speculate; Ellicott builds on the very identity Calvin waves away, since Peter renewed this temptation and met the self-same words.

debates.question: Why does the tone harden at this third attack?

positions.view: Because the disguise is dropped: earlier attacks were plausible and not directly against God's law, whereas now evil 'showed itself in its naked and absolute antagonism to the divine will', and Christ answers by naming the enemy.

debates.question: What did the angels do?

positions.view: Brought food and comfort, Wesley adding that they came 'to congratulate his victory' and Robertson that they cheered him in the reaction from the strain.
Declines to specify, warning against 'sensualising it as poets and artists have done', and notes their service came as the reward of the abnegation that had refused to test it.
They ministered as servants, which proves the Son's lordship over them.

outliers.view: Uses the answer against Rome's distinction between latreia and douleia, insisting that Christ 'rejects this frivolous distinction' by claiming for God the word for outward homage, so that the bodily as well as the inward worship belongs to him alone.

themes: And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me.
Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.
Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.

12.pericope_label: Now when Jesus had heard that John was cast into prison, he departed into Galilee

schools.summary: Ellicott lists what falls into the year-long gap from the fourth Gospel — the call of the first disciples, Cana, the cleansing of the Temple, Nicodemus, the Baptist's last testimony — and draws the inference the others miss, that the verse implies a Judaean ministry 'which for some reason the writer does not narrate'. Robertson calls the omitted stretch 'the year of obscurity' and notes that without John we should know nothing of it. Barnes denies the safety motive outright, since Jesus went straight into Herod's territory having given him no offence, and substitutes three others.

Calvin meets the apparent contradiction with John's Gospel, which has the Baptist and Christ teaching at once: the three evangelists pass over the overlap because the Baptist's course was preparatory and unfinished, so that although Christ taught within that period 'he did not, strictly speaking, begin to [teach] till he succeeded to John' — 'when the dawn was passed, the sun arose'. He ends on Luke's phrase rather than Matthew's, that Jesus came in the power of the Spirit, since we must not 'imagine Christ to have any thing about him that is earthly or human'. Gill names the prison from Josephus as the castle of Machaerus.
Wesley traces the itinerary between temptation and Galilee step by step, insisting 'this journey was not immediately after his temptation'.

Henry makes the timing deliberate: Christ did not move until John was silenced, since otherwise 'the minds of people would have been distracted between the two' — 'John must be Christ's harbinger, but not his rival', and 'the moon and stars are lost when the sun rises'. The succession is providential — 'Moses my servant is dead, John is cast into prison; now, therefore, Joshua, arise; Jesus, arise' — and the imprisonment is not mere circumstance: 'if John be cast into prison, Jesus hears it, takes cognizance of it, and steers his course accordingly.'

Chrysostom reads the withdrawal as instruction, teaching 'not to go to meet temptations, but to give place and withdraw ourselves', since 'it is no reproach, the not casting one's self into danger, but the failing to stand manfully when fallen into it'. He also notices the pattern that when Christ is about to turn to the Gentiles the occasion is always given him by Jews, who here 'thrust out Christ into the Galilee of the Gentiles'.
Rabanus reads it allegorically, John and the prophets being 'the voice going before the Word', so that 'when prophecy ceased and was fettered, then came the Word'.

debates.question: Why did Jesus withdraw into Galilee?

positions.view: As instruction in withdrawal — not to court danger, though not to flinch once in it.

Not for safety at all, since he entered Herod's own territory: rather because the people's attention was roused, John's work needed seconding, and beginning near Jerusalem would have drawn envy too soon.
Both — 'not only to provide for his own safety' but 'to supply the want of John Baptist, and to build upon the good foundation he had laid'.

debates.question: How is this to be reconciled with John's Gospel, where both preach at once?

positions.view: The synoptists pass over the overlap because the Baptist's course was preparatory; Christ taught within it but did not properly begin 'till he succeeded to John'.
The gap is simply unnarrated — a whole year, recoverable only from John, which Ellicott takes to imply a Judaean ministry Matthew chose not to record.

outliers.view: Alone makes the sequencing of the two ministries a matter of design rather than circumstance: John had to be eclipsed before Christ shone, or 'one would have said, I am of John, and another, I am of Jesus' — 'the moon and stars are lost when the sun rises'.

themes: Now when Jesus had heard that John was cast into prison, he departed into Galilee;

13.pericope_label: And leaving Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast, in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that Matthew 'records the bare fact' and supplies from Luke and John what he omits, then gives four reasons for Capernaum: its position as a garrison and custom-house town at the centre of the fishing trade, its nearness to Nazareth, its publicans and Gentiles 'not to be found in the more secluded villages', and the protection already secured by the healing of the officer's son. He can also report the Palestine Exploration Society's identification of the site with Tell-Hûm and its disinterred synagogue — 'possibly, therefore, the very synagogue, built by the believing centurion'. Barnes, writing earlier, still calls the site 'now uncertain', reporting a missionary who found only Arab huts there in 1823; Robertson gives the identification as settled. Lightfoot answers why Capernaum was Christ's own city by citing the Jewish scale of residence: thirty days makes a man liable to the alms-chest, twelve months to the taxes.

Calvin reads the move as a deliberate withdrawal — Christ had frequented Nazareth, and now 'in order to avoid danger, he now bade a final adieu to it' — and is careful about the district's name, explaining that Galilee is called of the Gentiles 'not only on account of its vicinity to Tyre and Sidon, but because its inhabitants were a mixture of Jews and Gentiles', correcting his own reference in the same sentence, since the cities granted to Hiram were Solomon's gift and not David's. Gill notes that Christ had first preached at Nazareth to the people's liking.

Clarke presses the compound verb into 'entirely leaving Nazareth', so that Christ 'utterly forsook' the place, and observes that Capernaum is famous throughout the New Testament and never mentioned in the Old, guessing it one of the cities built after the return from Babylon. Wesley gives the reason from Luke in a line: they had rejected his word and tried to kill him.

debates.question: Where was Capernaum?

positions.view: Unknown — 'the site it occupied is now uncertain', an American missionary in 1823 having found only twenty or thirty uninhabited Arab huts among the presumed ruins.
Tell-Hûm, identified by the Palestine Exploration Society, whose excavations uncovered a Roman-period building taken for the synagogue.

outliers.view: Alone explains why Capernaum could be called Christ's own city and why he paid the half-shekel there, quoting the graduated Jewish rule by which residence becomes citizenship: thirty days for the alms-chest, six months for clothing the poor, nine for burying them, and twelve for the ordinary taxes — 'how long does a man dwell in some city before he be as one of the citizens? Twelve months.'

themes: And leaving Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast, in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim:

14.pericope_label: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet... From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand

schools.summary: Barnes states the technical point plainly, that Matthew 'has given the sense, but not the very words', and takes the darkness as social as much as spiritual, Galileans being proverbially ignorant with 'a coarse, outlandish manner of speech' — from which he draws the compassion of a Saviour who chose 'to minister to the needy, the ignorant, and the contemned'. He and Clarke converge independently on the shadow of death as cast by a body standing between the nations and the sun. Robertson notes that Matthew applies words about deliverance from Assyria to the Messiah. Ellicott dates the beginning of the Galilean ministry to the autumn or winter between the Passovers of A.D. 26 and 27 and describes the method from Luke's representative scene. On 'beyond Jordan' Barnes denies the eastward sense that Wesley assumes.

Calvin alone admits the quotation is a problem — 'there is some appearance, as if Matthew had put a wrong meaning on the quotation from the prophet' — and answers by reading Isaiah in context: two calamities already fallen and a third foretold, against which the promise is that the last dimness will be less than the first. He rejects confining it to Jerusalem's escape from Sennacherib as 'very absurd', makes the return from Babylon the dawn and Christ the sunrise, and concludes that 'our souls are plunged in the darkness of everlasting death, till he enlightens them by his grace'. Gill reports that the Jews expected the Messiah in Galilee, an expectation that 'must be grounded on this prophecy'.

Clarke makes the chapter's best small observation, that Isaiah wrote of a people who walked in darkness while Matthew writes that they sat in it — the change deliberate, since sitting 'expresses a greater degree of intellectual blindness', so that after seven centuries they were worse off than when the prophet spoke. He confirms the Jewish expectation of a Galilean Messiah as 'a regular tradition', and makes repentance the rule for every commissioned preacher. Wesley builds a three-step descent from the same words — walked, then sat, then in the region of the shadow of death — and explains why the opening words could not differ from the Baptist's.

Pseudo-Chrysostom ties the beginning of preaching to what preceded it: the gospel belongs to one who has overcome hunger in the desert, despised covetousness on the mountain and rejected ambition in the temple. Cyril draws the lesson of timing — if the Master 'followed the right time in due order, ought we, His servants, to venture out of order?'

debates.question: What does it mean that Jesus 'began' to preach?

positions.view: It dates not from Capernaum nor from John's arrest but 'from the time that Satan left tempting him'.
The start of settled public work, Robertson noting he 'had been preaching for over a year already elsewhere'.
A datable season — the autumn or winter between the Passovers of A.D. 26 and 27.

debates.question: Does 'beyond Jordan' mean east of the river?

positions.view: No — it means near the Jordan, perhaps near its sources, not east of it.
Yes — 'that part of Galilee which lay beyond Jordan was so called'.

outliers.view: Alone treats the difference between Isaiah's walking and Matthew's sitting as intentional evidence of a worsened condition, since sitting in darkness 'expresses a greater degree of intellectual blindness, than walking in darkness does'.

themes: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying,
The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles;
The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up.
From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

18.pericope_label: And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea: for they were fishers

schools.summary: Ellicott insists that 'in no part of the Gospel history is it more necessary to remember St. John's record as we read that of the Three', and reconstructs the men's earlier life from it — Bethsaida, partnership in one trade, hopes quickened by the rising of Judas of Galilee, baptism by John, then a season as Christ's companions before he began his Galilean circuit alone 'and left them to return to their old calling'. He inclines to treating Luke's account as one event more fully told. Robertson attends to the tackle, the word being a casting-net thrown over the shoulder to open in a circle. Barnes describes the lake, stormy from the surrounding hills, its shores called by Josephus 'a perfect paradise'. Lightfoot supplies the law they worked under.

Calvin argues at length that Luke records the same occasion, and rests it on an argument the others do not use: if these men had been called earlier and gone back to the boats, 'it would follow that they were apostates, who had forsaken their Master, despised their calling'. From the dispute he draws a general principle, that 'no fixed and distinct order of dates was observed' by the evangelists, who 'disregard the order of time' and present the leading transactions in summary.

Clarke asks why not the eminent scribes, and answers that mean instruments made plain that 'the excellency of the power' was of God — then turns it on his own day's institutions: seminaries have real uses, but 'to make preachers of the Gospel is a matter to which they are utterly inadequate; it is a prerogative that God never did, and never will, delegate to man', and 'men-made ministers have almost ruined the heritage of God'.

Henry agrees the men were known to Christ beforehand and draws the lesson that 'Christ brings poor souls by degrees into fellowship with himself'. Arguing the same premise as Clarke about unlearned instruments, he guards the opposite flank: Christ 'sometimes chooses to endow those with the gifts of grace who have least to show of the gifts of nature', yet 'this will not justify the bold intrusion of ignorant and unqualified men into the work of the ministry'. His interest is where the call was issued — not to Herod's court, not to the chief priests, but to a lake in a despised province, so 'surely Christ sees not as man sees'.

Pseudo-Chrysostom explains the timing: the apostles were called 'before He spoke or did any thing', so that no word or deed should be hidden from them and they could afterwards say 'what we have seen and heard, that we cannot but speak'; their trade was itself a prophecy of their future work.

debates.question: Had the four been called before, and gone back to fishing?

positions.view: Yes — they had accepted him as the Christ months earlier and were left to return to their trade when he began his Galilean circuit alone.
No — if they had been called and had returned to the boats 'it would follow that they were apostates, who had forsaken their Master, despised their calling'.

debates.question: Does the unlearning of the first ministers license unlearned preachers?

positions.view: It licenses distrust of the institutions: to make preachers 'is a prerogative that God never did, and never will, delegate to man', and 'men-made ministers have almost ruined the heritage of God'.
It does not: God may endow those with least of nature's gifts, 'yet this will not justify the bold intrusion of ignorant and unqualified men into the work of the ministry'.

outliers.view: Supplies the law under which the men were working: among the ten conditions the rabbis credit to Joshua, any Israelite might 'spread his nets for fishing in the sea of Tiberias', but none might set up a wall obstructing shipping, since stakes and cane fences were 'not permitted, because it is an impediment to the ships'.

themes: And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea: for they were fishers.

19.pericope_label: And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men... and they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him

schools.summary: Ellicott hears in the summons 'in some sense the first parable in our Lord's teaching', the sea the evil world, souls the fish, the net the Church, and traces the image from Jeremiah's darker use to Clement's hymn — 'Fisher of men, the blest, / Out of the world's unrest'. He then refuses an apologetic argument available to him, declining to make the mending of nets an undesigned coincidence with Luke, since mending followed even an unsuccessful night and Luke's Greek says the nets were on the point of breaking, not that they broke. He reads the leaving of Zebedee sociologically, Mark's hired servants suggesting his sons were better off than the sons of Jona. Barnes reaches the cost by imagination; Robertson keeps to the verb for adjusting a net.

Calvin declines to explain the promptness psychologically. What strikes him is 'the power of Christ's voice' — not the voice alone, since 'those whom the Lord is pleased to lead and draw to himself, are inwardly addressed by his Spirit'. Gill has the men formerly John's disciples who had returned to their trade after the imprisonment, and totals what went with the nets: boats, trade, substance, relations, friends.

Clarke turns the metaphor against unfit ministers — those who 'presume to take the name of fishers of men, and know not how to cast the net of the Divine word' and who 'study not to catch men, but to catch money' — quoting Fletcher's fishing eclogue at them. On leaving the father he states the competing duty first, provision for parents being after God 'the highest duty we owe', then subordinates it, adding that if their support is not otherwise made up 'it is a proof we have mistaken our call'. He also defends the disciples against the sneer that men with only nets sacrificed little: 'he who has nothing but a net, and leaves that for the sake of doing good to the souls of men, leaves his All.'

debates.question: Is the mending of the nets an undesigned coincidence with Luke's account?

positions.view: No, twice over: mending and washing followed even a fruitless night, and Luke's Greek says the nets were on the point of breaking rather than that they broke.

debates.question: What did the four actually give up?

positions.view: Everything they had — 'he who has nothing but a net, and leaves that... leaves his All', and with the nets went boats, trade, substance and kin.
More than they knew: 'little did they know what awaited them, when they left their unmended nets to rot on the beach, and followed the unknown and unhonoured Jesus of Nazareth'.

outliers.view: Alone turns from rebuking the leaving of a father to congratulating him: what an honour the vocation of James and John was to old Zebedee, who, if pious, must have felt 'unutterable delight'.

themes: And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.
And they straightway left their nets, and followed him.
And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them.
And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him.

23.pericope_label: And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness

schools.summary: Barnes calls the origin of synagogues 'involved in much obscurity', reasoning that only sacrifice was confined to Jerusalem so other worship could happen anywhere, and adds the custom that matters here — the reader stood and the expounder sat, so 'our Saviour imitated their example, and was commonly seated'. Ellicott resists making the healings evidential, holding that Matthew records them 'not directly as evidence of a supernatural mission, but almost, so to speak, as the natural accompaniments of His work; signs, not of power only or chiefly, but of the love, tenderness, pity, which were the true marks... of the kingdom of heaven'. Robertson counts this the first of three Galilean circuits. Lightfoot traces the ten-man rule to the Talmud's definition of a great city.

Calvin's note on the lunatics is the chapter's most surprising: admitting that Greeks, Romans and Jews alike supposed such disorders followed the moon, he refuses to let Scripture be held responsible, since 'Scripture was not intended to determine questions of physical science, in which inductive reasoning is a sufficient guide, but to declare those truths, which could never have been known without an express revelation'. He is as careful with the demoniacs, restricting the term to those given up to Satan so that 'he holds possession of their minds and of their bodily senses', and scrupulous about scope — not everyone diseased was cured, but 'there was no class of diseases, that was ever presented to him, which he did not' heal. Gill notes the country's poverty and populousness.

Clarke dates synagogues after the return from Babylon and adds a detail nobody else has, that they were built 'especially by rivers, that they might have water for the convenience of their frequent washings'. He quotes Theophylact for the distinction between a chronic disorder and 'a temporary disorder of the body', insisting it 'is necessary to be observed'. Wesley adds that gospel means the joyous message, 'the proper name of our religion'.

Henry presses the physician image hardest. Some illnesses 'are called the reproach of physicians, being obstinate to all the methods they can prescribe; but even those were the glory of this Physician', his word 'the true panpharmacon'. He reads the three named afflictions as covering everything — palsy the greatest weakness of body, lunacy of mind, possession the greatest calamity of both — and explains the crowds by the terms offered, a physician 'so easy of access, so sure of success', who 'cured gratis, and took no fees, could not but have abundance of patients'.

Pseudo-Chrysostom explains the order: kings gather an army before war, so the Lord 'first collected Apostles, and then began to preach the Gospel'; and since the sick 'could not come to their physician, He as a zealous Physician went about to visit' them.

debates.question: How old are the synagogues?

positions.view: Their origin is 'involved in much obscurity', growing naturally out of non-sacrificial worship and the need for shelter.
'Not probably older than the return from the Babylonish captivity.'

debates.question: What are the healings for?

positions.view: Proof — such diseases 'cannot be healed by natural means', so curing them 'proved his divinity'.
Not chiefly evidence but accompaniment: 'signs, not of power only or chiefly, but of the love, tenderness, pity, which were the true marks... of the kingdom of heaven'.

outliers.view: Refuses to let the word for lunatic commit the evangelists to lunar medicine, on the principle that Scripture does not settle questions of physical science: the term no more binds them to the theory than ordinary talk of sunrise binds us to believing the sun moves and not the earth.

themes: And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people.

24.pericope_label: And his fame went throughout all Syria... And there followed him great multitudes of people from Galilee, and from Decapolis

schools.summary: Barnes argues in seven steps that the possessed were really possessed, against those who took the phrase for melancholy or epilepsy: Christ and the apostles managed them as persons, they spoke and confessed knowledge of Christ, which 'could not be said of diseases', they went out and entered others, and if Christ's belief here may be denied 'no other sentiment of his' is safe. On lunacy he keeps the name and drops the theory. Ellicott defers the question of possession to the Gadarene narrative, noting only that the word here is demon rather than the word used of the Tempter, and is precise about the palsy, whose name 'points, not to a view of the cause of the disease, but to its conspicuous phenomena'. Robertson traces torments back to the Lydian touchstone that tested gold, and notes the plural crowds — 'not just one crowd, but crowds and crowds'.
Gill quotes the rabbinic rule that 'there is no multitude less than sixty myriads', then warns against taking it literally here.

Clarke names and rejects the theory 'that the sacred writers accommodated themselves to the unfounded prejudices of the common people', which 'can never comport with the accounts given of these persons'. He presses the grammatical point that the English plural devils is wrong, the Greek word being 'not found in the plural in any part of the Sacred Writings, when speaking of evil spirits' — demons are many, the Devil one. Uniquely, he defends the lunar theory as physically true, since at new and full moon sun and moon act together on the atmosphere. He also reads the crowds as a recognised Messianic sign, answering the famine of Amos, 'not a famine of bread, but of hearing the words of the Lord'. Wesley calls Syria the whole province, 'of which the Jewish country was only a small part'.

debates.question: Were the demoniacs really possessed, or is the language accommodation?

positions.view: Really possessed — Barnes giving seven arguments from how Christ and the apostles addressed them, Clarke rejecting the accommodation theory as one that 'can never comport with the accounts given of these persons'.
Defers the question to the Gadarene narrative, observing only that the possessed are grouped with the lunatics yet distinguished from them.

debates.question: Does the moon affect the disease that bears its name?

positions.view: Yes, and by a stated mechanism: at new and full moon the sun and moon act together on the atmosphere, producing tides and, in sensitive constitutions, real change.
The name was given 'because it was formerly imagined' so; 'it is not certain that the moon has any effect', but 'no harm arises from the use of the name'.
Report the belief without endorsing it, Ellicott noting that Eastern travellers dreaded a stroke of moon almost as much as of sun.

debates.question: Which cities made up the Decapolis?

positions.view: Damascus was its metropolis and most ancient city, and the district lay on both sides of Jordan.
Scythopolis was chief and the only one west of the river; Damascus is merely one of two possible members.
Pliny's list includes Damascus, but Josephus's calling Scythopolis the largest makes it 'almost certain that he did not include Damascus' at all.

outliers.view: Stands alone in defending the lunar theory of epilepsy as physically true, and in rejecting outright the principle of accommodation that Calvin had used on the same word one verse earlier.

themes: And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them.
And there followed him great multitudes of people from Galilee, and from Decapolis, and from Jerusalem, and from Judea, and from beyond Jordan.
